content: 1. Piperacillin may interfere with the therapeutic effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors. Close monitoring is recommended when co-administering these agents. 2. Chloramphenicol reduces the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 3. Bacteriostatic agents can inhibit the effects of bactericidal agents like piperacillin. Use caution and monitor closely. 4. Chlorothiazide increases piperacillin levels by reducing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 5. Co-administration of piperacillin with the cholera vaccine should be avoided due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Systemic antibiotics may act against the vaccine strain, reducing its efficacy. Avoid administering the cholera vaccine to patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. 6. Piperacillin increases the levels or effects of choline magnesium trisalicylate by competing for renal tubular clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 7. Salicylate salts may be displaced from protein-binding sites or displace other highly protein-bound drugs, such as penicillins. Monitor closely. 8. Clarithromycin reduces the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 9. Piperacillin decreases the effects of cosibelimab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 10. Piperacillin increases the effects of dalteparin by enhancing anticoagulation. Avoid or use an alternative drug. Piperacillin can also inhibit platelet aggregation. 11. Demeclocycline reduces the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 12. Dichlorphenamide and piperacillin both decrease serum potassium levels. Use caution and monitor closely. 13. Piperacillin decreases the effects of dostarlimab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 14. Doxycycline reduces the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 15. Piperacillin decreases the effects of durvalumab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 16. Piperacillin increases the effects of enoxaparin by enhancing anticoagulation. Avoid or use an alternative drug. Piperacillin can also inhibit platelet aggregation. 17. Erythromycin base reduces the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 18. Erythromycin ethylsuccinate reduces the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 19. Erythromycin lactobionate reduces the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 20. Erythromycin stearate reduces the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 21. Piperacillin increases the effects of gentamicin through pharmacodynamic synergism. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 22. Piperacillin increases the levels or effects of heparin by enhancing anticoagulation. Avoid or use an alternative drug. Piperacillin can also inhibit platelet aggregation. 23. Hydrochlorothiazide increases piperacillin levels by reducing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 24. Piperacillin increases the levels or effects of ibuprofen IV by competing for renal tubular clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 25. Piperacillin increases the levels or effects of meclofenamate by competing for renal tubular clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 26. Piperacillin decreases the effects of microbiota oral therapy through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid or use an alternative drug. Antibacterial agents may reduce the efficacy of microbiota oral therapy by acting against bacterial spores. Complete antibiotic regimens 2–4 days before initiating microbiota oral therapy. 27. Minocycline reduces the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 28. Piperacillin increases the effects of neomycin PO through pharmacodynamic synergism. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 29. Piperacillin decreases the effects of nivolumab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 30. Omadacycline reduces the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid or use an alternative drug. Tetracyclines may interfere with the bactericidal action of penicillins. Monitor for reduced therapeutic effects of penicillins when used concomitantly with tetracyclines. 31. Piperacillin decreases the effects of pembrolizumab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 32. Piperacillin decreases the effects of penpulimab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 33. Probenecid increases the levels or effects of piperacillin by competing for renal tubular clearance. Use caution and monitor closely. 34. Piperacillin decreases the effects of retifanlimab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 35. Rose hips increase the levels or effects of piperacillin by competing for renal tubular clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 36. Sarecycline reduces the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid or use an alternative drug. Tetracyclines may interfere with the bactericidal action of penicillins. Monitor for reduced therapeutic effects of penicillins when used concomitantly with tetracyclines. 37. Piperacillin decreases the effects of sintilimab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 38. Piperacillin decreases the effects of sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. Antibiotics may reduce efficacy by altering colonic bacterial flora needed to convert sodium picosulfate to its active form. 39. Piperacillin increases the effects of streptomycin through pharmacodynamic synergism. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 40. Tetracycline reduces the effects of piperacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 41. Piperacillin decreases the effects of tislelizumab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 42. Piperacillin increases the effects of tobramycin through pharmacodynamic synergism. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 43. Piperacillin decreases the effects of toripalimab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 44. Piperacillin increases the toxicity of vancomycin through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. Monitor kidney function in patients receiving both piperacillin and vancomycin. 45. Piperacillin increases the toxicity of vecuronium through pharmacodynamic synergism. Modify therapy and monitor closely. Neuromuscular blockade may be prolonged. 46. Piperacillin and warfarin may increase each other’s effects through pharmacodynamic synergism. Modify therapy and monitor closely. Platelet dysfunction may occur with extended-spectrum penicillins. Monitor INR and adjust warfarin dose if needed. 47. Piperacillin increases the levels or effects of willow bark by competing for renal tubular clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 48. Piperacillin contains sodium (5 mg of Na+ per gram), which should be considered in patients requiring restricted salt intake. Periodic electrolyte determinations are recommended in patients with low potassium reserves, and the possibility of hypokalemia should be considered in patients receiving cytotoxic therapy or diuretics. 49. Piperacillin has been identified as an independent risk factor for renal failure and is associated with delayed recovery of renal function compared to other beta-lactam antibiotics. If alternative treatment options are inadequate or unavailable, monitor renal function during treatment. 50. Combined use of piperacillin and vancomycin may increase the incidence of acute kidney injury. 51. Serious skin reactions, including toxic epidermal necrolysis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, acute exanthematous pustulosis, and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), have been reported. Monitor closely if a rash develops and discontinue therapy if lesions progress. 52. Leukopenia and neutropenia may occur during prolonged therapy. Monitor hematologic tests during extended treatment. 53. Use of piperacillin may result in fungal or bacterial superinfection. Prescribing therapy in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a prophylactic indication is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. 54. Dosage adjustment is recommended in patients with renal impairment or those receiving hemodialysis. 55. Therapy has been associated with an increased incidence of fever and rash in cystic fibrosis patients. 56. Piperacillin and tazobactam cross the placenta in humans. However, there is insufficient data in pregnant women to inform a drug-associated risk for major birth defects and miscarriage. No fetal structural abnormalities were observed in animal studies when piperacillin/tazobactam was administered intravenously during organogenesis at doses 1–3 times the human dose based on body surface area. However, fetotoxicity in the presence of maternal toxicity was observed in developmental toxicity and peri/postnatal studies in rats. 57. Piperacillin is excreted in human milk, but tazobactam concentrations in human milk have not been studied. There is no information on the effects of piperacillin and tazobactam on the breastfed child or milk production. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be considered along with the mother’s clinical need for therapy and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed child from therapy or the underlying maternal condition. 58. Piperacillin inhibits the biosynthesis of cell wall mucopeptides during active multiplication and has antipseudomonal activity. 59. Piperacillin has a half-life of 36–80 minutes, which is dose-dependent and prolonged in renal insufficiency. It is 16% protein-bound, with 70–80% absorption when administered intramuscularly. It crosses the placenta, is metabolized in the liver, and is excreted primarily in urine and partially in feces. 60. Piperacillin is compatible with common solvents and additives such as clindamycin, flucloxacillin, fluconazole, hydrocortisone, linezolid, ofloxacin, potassium chloride, and verapamil. It is also compatible with certain Y-site drugs, including allopurinol, bivalirudin, ciprofloxacin, diltiazem, esmolol, famotidine, heparin, hydromorphone, linezolid, lorazepam, magnesium sulfate, meperidine, midazolam, morphine, ranitidine, verapamil, and zidovudine. 61. Piperacillin should be reconstituted with compatible diluents such as sterile water for injection, bacteriostatic water for injection, normal saline, or dextrose 5% water. Slight darkening of the solution does not indicate potency loss. Administer via slow direct injection over 3–5 minutes or intermittent infusion in at least 50 mL over 20–30 minutes. For intramuscular administration, inject into the upper outer quadrant of the buttock.
